title: Vitamin D — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: The Food and Nutrition Board at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has established Recommended Dietary Allowances and Adequate Intakes for vitamin D. These values range from 15 to 20 mcg (600–800 IU) for adults and from 10 to 15 mcg (400–600 IU) for infants, children, and adolescents, depending on age.

title: Vitamin D — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: Vitamin D is found naturally in a few foods, such as the flesh of fatty fish, fish liver oils, beef liver, egg yolks, and cheese. In American diets, fortified foods (e.g., milk, breakfast cereals) provide most of the vitamin D.

title: Vitamin D — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
section: Groups at Risk of Vitamin D Inadequacy
text: Certain groups of people are more likely than others to have inadequate vitamin D status. These include breastfed infants, older adults, people with limited sun exposure, people with dark skin, people with conditions that limit fat absorption, and people with obesity or those who have undergone gastric bypass surgery.

title: Vitamin D — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
section: Health Risks from Excessive Vitamin D
text: Vitamin D toxicity can cause hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and high serum 25(OH)D concentrations; in extreme cases, it may lead to renal failure, calcification of soft tissues, cardiac arrhythmias, and death. Vitamin D toxicity is almost always a result of excessive intakes of vitamin D through supplements. Taking calcium supplements in combination with vitamin D supplements may increase the risk of certain adverse effects. The Tolerable Upper Intake Level for vitamin D ranges from 25 to 100 mcg (1,000–4,000 IU), depending on age.

title: Magnesium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: What magnesium does in the body
text: Magnesium is important for many processes in the body, including regulating muscle and nerve function, blood sugar levels, and blood pressure and making protein, bone, and DNA.

title: Magnesium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: How much magnesium do I need? Average daily recommended amounts in milligrams (mg) (table)
text: Men 400–420 mg Women 310–320 mg

title: Magnesium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: You can get recommended amounts of magnesium by eating a variety of foods, including the following: Legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains, and green leafy vegetables (such as spinach)

title: Magnesium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: Side effects of high supplement doses
text: High intakes of magnesium from dietary supplements and medications can cause diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal cramping.

title: Magnesium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Bisphosphonates, used to treat osteoporosis, are not well absorbed when taken too soon before or after taking dietary supplements or medications with high amounts of magnesium.

title: Iron — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: How much iron do I need? Recommended amount (table)
text: Adult men 19–50 years 8 mg Adult women 19–50 years 18 mg Adults 51 years and older 8 mg

title: Iron — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: You can get recommended amounts of iron by eating a variety of foods, including the following: Lean meat, seafood, and poultry Iron-fortified breakfast cereals and breads White beans, lentils, spinach, kidney beans, and peas Nuts and some dried fruits, such as raisins

title: Iron — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: However, certain groups of people are more likely than others to have trouble getting enough iron: Teen girls and women with heavy periods Pregnant women and teens Infants (especially if they are premature or low-birth weight) Frequent blood donors People with cancer, gastrointestinal (GI) disorders, or heart failure

title: Iron — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: Can iron be harmful? Daily upper limits for iron from all sources (table)
text: Ages Upper Limit Birth to 12 months 40 mg Children 1–13 years 40 mg Teens 14–18 years 45 mg Adults 19+ years 45 mg

title: Calcium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: What calcium does in the body
text: Your body needs calcium for muscles to move and for nerves to carry messages between your brain and every part of your body.

title: Calcium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Milk, yogurt, and cheese are the main food sources of calcium for most people in the United States.

title: Calcium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Calcium is absorbed best when you take 500 mg or less at one time.

title: Calcium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: High levels of calcium in the blood and urine can cause poor muscle tone, poor kidney function, low phosphate levels, constipation, nausea, weight loss, extreme tiredness, frequent need to urinate, abnormal heart rhythms, and a high risk of death from heart disease.

title: Zinc — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: How much zinc do I need? Average daily recommended amounts in milligrams (mg) (table)
text: Adult males 11 mg Adult females 8 mg

title: Zinc — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Oysters, which have very high amounts of zinc. Meat, fish, poultry, seafood such as crab and lobsters, and fortified breakfast cereals are also good sources of zinc.

title: Zinc — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Yes, too much zinc can be harmful. Signs of too much zinc include nausea, dizziness, headaches, upset stomach, vomiting, and loss of appetite.

title: Vitamin B12 — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Vitamin B12 is a nutrient that helps keep your body's blood and nerve cells healthy and helps make DNA, the genetic material in all of your cells.

title: Vitamin B12 — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Fish, meat, poultry, eggs, milk, and other dairy products contain vitamin B12.

title: Vitamin B12 — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Some breakfast cereals, nutritional yeasts, and other food products are fortified with vitamin B12.

title: Vitamin B12 — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: Am I getting enough vitamin B12?
text: People who eat little or no animal foods, such as vegetarians and vegans, might not get enough vitamin B12 from their diets.

title: Vitamin B12 — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: Am I getting enough vitamin B12?
text: Many older adults don't have enough hydrochloric acid in their stomach to absorb the vitamin B12 that's naturally present in food.

title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: The three main omega-3 fatty acids are alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: The AHA does not recommend omega-3 supplements for people who do not have a high risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Any side effects from taking omega-3 supplements are usually mild. They include an unpleasant taste in the mouth, bad breath, heartburn, nausea, stomach discomfort, diarrhea, headache, and smelly sweat.

title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: Do omega-3s interact with medications or other dietary supplements?
text: Omega-3 dietary supplements may interact with the medications you take. For example, high doses of omega-3s may cause bleeding problems when taken with warfarin (Coumadin) or other anticoagulant medicines.

title: Potassium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
section: What is potassium and what does it do?
text: Your body needs potassium for almost everything it does, including proper kidney and heart function, muscle contraction, and nerve transmission.

title: Potassium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: Fruits, such as dried apricots, prunes, raisins, orange juice, and bananas Vegetables, such as acorn squash, potatoes, spinach, tomatoes, and broccoli Lentils, kidney beans, soybeans, and nuts Milk and yogurt Meats, poultry, and fish

title: Potassium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
text: ACE inhibitors, such as benazepril (Lotensin), and angiotensin receptor blockers, such as losartan (Cozaar), are used to treat high blood pressure, heart disease, and kidney disease. They decrease the amount of potassium lost in the urine and can make potassium levels too high, especially in people who have kidney problems.

title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: Studies in both laboratory and sports settings have found that short-term creatine supplementation (for 5 to 7 days) in both men and women often significantly increases strength (e.g., for bench presses) and power (e.g., for cycling), work involving multiple sets of maximal effort muscle contractions, and sprinting and soccer performance.

title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: Many studies have shown that caffeine might enhance performance in athletes when they ingest about 2–6 mg/kg body weight before exercise by improving endurance, strength, and power in high-intensity team sports activities.

title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: Beetroot has generally improved performance and endurance to different extents compared with placebo among runners, swimmers, rowers, and cyclists in time trials and time-to-exhaustion tests, but not in all studies.

title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: Some studies suggest that beta-alanine consumption could provide small performance benefits in competitive events requiring high-intensity effort over a short period, such as rowing, swimming, and team sports (e.g., hockey and football) that involve repeated sprints and intermittent activity.

title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
text: Protein Builds, maintains, and repairs muscle Numerous clinical trials Research findings: Optimizes muscle training response during exercise and subsequent recovery period No safety concerns reported at daily recommended intakes for athletes of up to about 2.0 g/kg body weight (e.g., 136 g for a person weighing 150 lb)

title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
section: Antioxidants (vitamin C, vitamin E, and coenzyme Q10)
text: Studies suggest that the use of large doses of antioxidant supplements, especially vitamins C and E, may actually reduce rather than promote some of the beneficial effects of exercise.

title: Exercise and Physical Fitness
text: Regular exercise is one of the best things you can do for your health.

title: Exercise and Physical Fitness
text: Aerobic exercises such as walking, running, or swimming are sometimes referred to as cardio.

title: Exercise and Physical Fitness
text: Strength, or resistance training, exercises use weights, resistance bands, or your own body weight to build stronger muscles.

title: Exercise and Physical Fitness
text: Balance exercises, such as tai chi or standing on one leg, improve your stability and coordination.

title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults (Morton et al., Br J Sports Med, 2018)
text: Dietary protein supplementation significantly enhanced changes in muscle strength and size during prolonged RET in healthy adults. Increasing age reduces and training experience increases the efficacy of protein supplementation during RET. With protein supplementation, protein intakes at amounts greater than ~1.6 g/kg/day do not further contribute RET-induced gains in FFM.

title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults (Morton et al., Br J Sports Med, 2018)
text: Protein supplementation beyond total protein intakes of 1.62 g/kg/day resulted in no further RET-induced gains in FFM.

title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis (Schoenfeld et al., J Sports Sci, 2017)
text: The findings indicate a graded dose-response relationship whereby increases in RT volume produce greater gains in muscle hypertrophy.

title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis (Schoenfeld et al., J Sports Sci, 2017)
text: Each additional set was associated with an increase in effect size (ES) of 0.023 corresponding to an increase in the percentage gain by 0.37%.

title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Schoenfeld et al., Sports Med, 2016)
text: When comparing studies that investigated training muscle groups between 1 to 3 days per week on a volume-equated basis, the current body of evidence indicates that frequencies of training twice a week promote superior hypertrophic outcomes to once a week. It can therefore be inferred that the major muscle groups should be trained at least twice a week to maximize muscle growth; whether training a muscle group three times per week is superior to a twice-per-week protocol remains to be determined.

title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Schoenfeld et al., Sports Med, 2016)
text: Analysis using binary frequency as a predictor variable revealed a significant impact of training frequency on hypertrophy effect size (P = 0.002), with higher frequency being associated with a greater effect size than lower frequency (0.49 ± 0.08 vs. 0.30 ± 0.07, respectively).

title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine (Kreider et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2017)
text: These studies show that short and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well-tolerated in healthy individuals and in a number of patient populations ranging from infants to the elderly.

title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine (Kreider et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2017)
text: Studies have consistently shown that creatine supplementation increases intramuscular creatine concentrations which may help explain the observed improvements in high intensity exercise performance leading to greater training adaptations.

title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise (Jäger et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2017)
text: For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance, an overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4-2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is sufficient for most exercising individuals, a value that falls in line within the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range published by the Institute of Medicine for protein.

title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise (Jäger et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2017)
text: The optimal time period during which to ingest protein is likely a matter of individual tolerance, since benefits are derived from pre- or post-workout ingestion; however, the anabolic effect of exercise is long-lasting (at least 24 h), but likely diminishes with increasing time post-exercise.

title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise (Jäger et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2017)
text: Recommendations regarding the optimal protein intake per serving for athletes to maximize MPS are mixed and are dependent upon age and recent resistance exercise stimuli. General recommendations are 0.25 g of a high-quality protein per kg of body weight, or an absolute dose of 20-40 g.

title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise (Jäger et al., J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2017)
text: Pre-sleep casein protein intake (30-40 g) provides increases in overnight MPS and metabolic rate without influencing lipolysis.
